paras: The lynching of Davis Sabini was the hanging of a 22-year-old Italian man by residents of Cortez, Nevada, in November 1888, after he was accused of fatally shooting Richard "Dick" Holt in a quarrel over a loan. The men involved told a deputy sheriff that Sabini had hanged himself, and a coroner's jury returned a verdict of suicide that the Elko Independent openly doubted. The story ran as a brief wire item in papers across the country, and in Cortez it led the town's Italian residents to threaten revenge.

Cortez was a mining camp about ninety miles from Austin, Nevada, the site of the Wenban mine and its mill. According to the Austin Reveille, Sabini shot Holt at about 10 p.m. in Lower Cortez after Holt said his loans to Sabini came to more than thirty dollars; Sabini claimed self-defense.

The Austin wire dispatch said more simply that Sabini shot Holt in the stomach because he could not get a loan, and that Holt died within twenty-four hours, asking that the court hang his killer. The dispatch described Holt as well liked and Sabini as a man of "unsavory reputation" who had been in several shooting scrapes.

In the Reveille's account, people rushed into the room after the shot, and John Engstrom drew a pistol and ordered Sabini to drop his weapon. Sabini ran for the door but was caught, disarmed and bound, and "a number of excited persons" took him toward the mill. The Reveille wrote that Holt's friends took justice into their own hands and strangled Sabini from a tree or a beam in the mill, while the wire dispatch said he was hoisted by the neck from the limb of a tree near the mill.

Deputy Sheriff W. J. Higby later found the body tied to a bedpost at a boarding house, some ten hours dead, with the knot under the left ear and the rope cut into the neck. The Elko Daily Independent, drawing on the Reveille, said the citizens had hanged him until he was dead and then hung the body from a bedpost "to indicate" suicide.

Coroner Joseph Moss came from Austin and held an inquest at Cortez on a Sunday morning. All six witnesses testified that Sabini had killed himself but gave no particulars, and no one would help Moss bury the body. The jury, whose members included a John Engstrom, found that "Davis Sabini committed suicide by hanging."

Italian residents of Cortez threatened to burn the mine property and mill and to shoot on sight anyone who had taken part in the lynching. The mine management armed its employees, and miners and mill men discussed ordering the Italians out of the district. No report of arrests, indictments or a trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The full Austin dispatch ran in the Los Angeles Herald under "Lynching in Nevada. A Cold-Blooded Murder Spedily Avenged" and in the Carson Morning Appeal under "Strung up to a tree. An Italian Murderer Gets His Deserts at Cortez." A shorter wire version reached papers from Seattle and Butte to Wisconsin and Vermont, with the victim's name garbled as "Ralasni," "Ralizno," "Rolsane" or "Balsani." Because of the Austin dateline, several of these papers moved the event to Texas, and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer headed it "A Texas Murderer Lynched."

Nevada papers carried fuller local accounts, most of them drawn from the Austin Reveille. The Reveille, as reprinted in the Central Nevadan, said it opposed mob law but judged the Cortez citizens' course justifiable, calling the camp "a regular slaughter pen" where the courts had let murderers escape. The Elko Independent took a different line on the inquest, writing that when a lynched man is found to have "committed suicide by hanging" there is "something wrong."

The papers disagree on the day of the shooting: the Austin dispatch said Wednesday evening, the Reveille Tuesday at about 10 p.m., and the Elko Independent's later note "last Friday." The Silver State placed Cortez in Lander County, while the Record-Union and the Morning Appeal placed it in Eureka County.

reader.title: Lynching of Davis Sabini
bases: Davis Sabini, accused of shooting Richard Holt, was seized by Cortez residents and hanged near the mill (A1, A11, A16).

Sabini was hanged without legal process by 'the citizens', 'a number of men' or 'a mob' (A11, A13, A22), who in the Reveille's account were Holt's friends acting to see justice done for the shooting (A16); the participants' claim of suicide and the coroner's suicide verdict were reported but not credited by any paper (A1, A18, A24).

The Austin dispatch based on the deputy sheriff's report (A1, A9) and the Austin Reveille's account (A11, A16) agree that Sabini was hanged by residents after shooting Holt; the only counter-version is the participants' and inquest witnesses' claim of suicide (A1, A24).

accounts.label: Austin wire dispatch (from the deputy sheriff)
accounts.gist: Sabini shot Holt over a refused loan; 'parties' hanged him from a tree near the mill; the deputy found the body tied to a bedpost and the men said it was suicide.

accounts.label: Austin Reveille
accounts.gist: Sabini was disarmed and bound by bystanders after the shooting, taken toward the mill by excited persons, and strangled by Holt's friends, who then pretended suicide; the editor called it justifiable.

accounts.label: Participants and inquest witnesses
accounts.gist: Sabini committed suicide by hanging; the coroner's jury so found.

framing.detail: Headlines 'A Cold-Blooded Murder Spedily Avenged' and 'An Italian Murderer Gets His Deserts at Cortez' presented the lynching as deserved punishment.
The Austin Reveille opposed 'mob law' in principle but called the Cortez citizens' course justifiable because the camp had become 'a regular slaughter pen' where courts failed.
The Elko Independent reported that the citizens lynched Sabini and said 'there is something wrong' with the suicide verdict, without condemning the lynching itself.
National papers ran a two- or three-sentence wire with garbled names and, in some, the place moved to Texas.

conflicts.note: The Austin dispatch of 10 November and the Reveille are earlier and closer to the source; a Friday date is hard to square with news reaching Austin on 10 November.

versions.value: Hanged from a tree limb near the Cortez mill
Strangled from a tree or a beam in the mill
Suicide by hanging (participants, inquest witnesses, coroner's jury)

conflicts.note: Every paper that reports the suicide claim presents it as a cover story; the knot under the ear and the body moved to a bedpost are cited against it.
The Texas placement is a wire error from the 'Austin' dateline.

record_check.dossier: The shooting was on a Tuesday or Wednesday before 10 November 1888 and the lynching followed before news reached Austin on 10 November; 16 November is a reporting date.

record_check.dossier: One lynching victim, Davis Sabini; the other names are spellings of Sabini except Dick Holt, the man Sabini was accused of shooting.
The papers call Sabini 'an Italian' and use no race term.
Lander per the Silver State; Eureka per the Record-Union and Morning Appeal.
One death by lynching (Sabini); Holt died of the gunshot that led to it.
Unnamed residents of Cortez: 'the citizens', Holt's friends, 'a number of excited persons'.
Caught, disarmed and bound by bystanders at the scene and taken toward the mill; no officer held him.
Holt's dying wish that the court hang his killer; the Reveille called the lynching justifiable because Cortez courts had failed to convict murderers.

info: Holt was shot on a Tuesday (Reveille) or Wednesday (Austin dispatch) evening before 10 November 1888, died about 24 hours later, and Sabini was hanged before the news reached Austin on 10 November; the Elko Independent later said Holt was killed 'last Friday'.
Cortez, Nevada, about ninety miles from Austin; the shooting was in Lower Cortez and the hanging near the Cortez (Wenban) mill.
One lynching victim: Davis (or David) Sabini, an Italian, aged 22; name spelled Saban, Sabani, Sabanio, Ralasni, Ralsani, Roliuzo, Ralizno, Rolsane and Balsani in different papers.
Accused of shooting Richard (Dick) Holt in the stomach after Holt refused to lend him money; Holt died about 24 hours later. Sabini claimed Holt owed him money and that he fired in self-defense.
Unnamed: 'parties' (dispatch), 'the citizens' (Elko), 'a number of excited persons' and Holt's friends (Reveille), 'a mob' (Walker Lake), the 'necktie party' (Morning Appeal).
